what_tested.framing: This report previews a proposed change where one general-traffic lane on a Toronto corridor would become a bicycle-only lane. The study looks at how this reallocation of road space could affect drivers, cyclists, and nearby residents and businesses.

glosses.car_commuter: Most car commuters are unaffected, but a small group of specific commuters absorbs a real delay, and access is slightly worse.
glosses.cyclist: Cyclists see no typical travel time change, slightly better access with low confidence, and a safety near-miss magnitude present but directionally not claimed.
glosses.pedestrian: Pedestrians see no change in typical travel time, may experience a subtle improvement in access, though the safety signal is too uncertain to interpret.
glosses.local_resident: A near-miss magnitude is present for this group, but its direction is not seed-stable and is not claimed here — the table shows the magnitude only.
glosses.business_owner: Access is estimated to be slightly worse for this group, from a low-confidence rule-based estimate.
glosses.accessibility: There isn't enough measurable signal in this run to characterize how this change affects accessibility.
glosses.transit_riders: There isn't enough measurable signal in this run to characterize how this change affects transit riders.

groups.label: Drivers
groups.synthesis: Some drivers worry that removing a car lane could add time to their trips, affecting their work or schedules. Others are relieved that their own commute times stay the same and hope the street outside their home or near the school will become quieter. A few express unease about the direction of the change, even if it doesn't affect them personally.

quotes.label: Rideshare / delivery driver
quotes.comment: That extra 1.8 minutes might not sound like much, but for me it's less trips per hour and more angry passengers. This lane change is just going to slow me down and cost me money.

quotes.label: Resident who drives the corridor
quotes.comment: Since my drive time stays about the same, I'm not too bothered by the change—and honestly, if it means less speeding and noise outside my front door, I might even be a little happier with the trade-off.

groups.label: Cyclists
groups.synthesis: Cyclists welcome the protected bike lane as a long-awaited improvement that reduces stress from car traffic without slowing them down. Many express relief at no longer being squeezed by cars, and some say they would start using the corridor regularly for the first time. The shared hope is for a calmer, less harried ride.

quotes.label: Bicycle delivery courier
quotes.comment: Same travel time but way less stress from cars zooming past me? That's a win in my book. I'll take a calmer ride any day.

quotes.label: Cautious newer rider
quotes.comment: I'm thrilled about the protected bike lane—I'd feel much safer biking here and might actually start using this corridor regularly instead of avoiding it.

groups.label: Pedestrians
groups.synthesis: Many walk-to-transit commuters are neutral, noting their own trip remains unchanged. A recurring hope is that the bike lane will calm traffic and make crossing streets feel less stressful, especially for those with children. Some supporters explicitly welcome a small time trade-off for that perceived benefit.

quotes.label: Walk-to-transit commuter
quotes.comment: Well, if my walking time and bus schedule aren't affected, I don't really mind the change—it's fine by me.

quotes.label: School-run parent on foot
quotes.comment: I'm happy about this change—any move that calms traffic and makes crossings safer for my kids is a win in my book, even if my walk time stays the same.

groups.label: Community voices
groups.synthesis: Business owners along the corridor worry that replacing parking with bike lanes will hurt curb access for customers and deliveries, while residents and some advocates hope the change will slow traffic and make the street more livable. Transit users express concern about potential delays to bus service but are open to benefits if traffic calming doesn't slow their commute. A recurring tension is between those who prioritize parking and car access for commerce and those who want a calmer, more pedestrian- and bike-friendly street.

quotes.label: Small business owner
quotes.comment: This bike lane is going to kill my business—my customers need to park right out front, and deliveries will be a nightmare.

quotes.label: Long-time corridor resident
quotes.comment: I've lived here for years, and anything that slows down traffic and makes the street safer for walking and biking is welcome in my book — I'm tired of the noise and speed.

cannot_tell.intro: The following limits define what this preview can and cannot claim, and should be read alongside the findings.

caveats.title: Safety direction is not established
caveats.body: The safety surrogate is reported as a magnitude only — its direction is not claimed: “sign not stable across seeds 42/43/44; directional claim not supported”. Do not read the safety column as 'the change made things safer or more dangerous'.

caveats.title: Surrogate measures are not crash predictions
caveats.body: Safety here means trajectory-derived surrogates (time-to-collision, hard braking, blocked junctions), counted as near-miss events observed in this run. They are not crashes, and this tool does not predict crashes, injuries, or their probability.

caveats.title: One corridor, one demand level
caveats.body: The simulation is bounded to a single corridor at a single modelled demand (300 cars, 82 bicycles, 129 pedestrians). It does not model the wider network, other times of day, or induced demand.

caveats.title: In-run adaptation is not settled equilibrium
caveats.body: Travelers do not re-plan across days here: 0 cars rerouted within the run. Real corridors reach a new equilibrium over weeks as people adjust routes, modes, and times — this preview shows the immediate response, not that settled state.

caveats.title: A stratified sample, not a census
caveats.body: The voiced reactions come from a stratified sample of personas pinned to specific simulated travelers (deliberately including the hardest-hit tail), not a poll of everyone. They show the texture of who wins and loses, never a headcount of support or opposition.

caveats.title: The access column is a rule-based estimate
caveats.body: Access impacts are a deterministic heuristic from the change type (e.g. curbside space), labelled low-confidence — an estimate to reason about, not a measurement.

violations.sentence: Most car commuters see no change in travel time, but a small group becomes markedly slower, while access is slightly worse and a safety signal is present but directionally unreliable.
A recurring hope is that the change will calm traffic and make the street safer, especially near a school, though a few worry that removing a car lane is a step in the wrong direction.
